title: Lesson 2: How LLMs Work for Implementers: Tokens, Context, Inference, Temperature
description: The four knobs that decide every LLM bill, latency budget, and reliability call: what tokens actually are, how the context window constrains agents, how inference really runs, and what temperature does and doesn't do.

questions.question: Why does the same information cost more tokens when written as JSON than as prose?
options: Braces, quotes, and colons each tend to become their own token
The model must translate the JSON into natural language before reading it
JSON requires a larger context window to store
JSON is encrypted before the model reads it
questions.explanation: Tokenizers tend to break structural characters into their own tokens, so the same facts cost roughly twice as much when formatted as JSON.

questions.question: Where should debugging start when an agent gives inconsistent or wrong answers?
options: Lower the temperature so the model samples more deterministically
Increase the maximum output token limit
Check that the needed information is present in the context
Switch to a larger and more capable model tier
questions.explanation: Temperature only reshapes how the model samples among what it already knows; it cannot supply information that is missing from the context or buried where the model will not use it.

questions.question: A response is slow before the first token appears. Which phase is the bottleneck?
options: Decode, where output tokens are generated one at a time
Temperature, which adds randomness to each sampling step
Caching, which reprocesses the static prefix on every call
Prefill, where the whole input is processed first
questions.explanation: Prefill processes the whole input to produce the first token, so a slow start points to a prompt that is too long; slowness while streaming is a decode problem instead.
